issues.legal_issue: The one-year limit for making a declaration of public purpose runs to the making of the declaration, not its later publication in the official gazette.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette on 4 June 1992, and the substance of the notification was subsequently published locally, including in newspapers on 17 and 19 May 1993.
The declaration was made on 17 May 1994 and published in the official gazette on 24 May 1994.
The High Court treated the gazette publication of the declaration, rather than the date it was made, as decisive and quashed the acquisition proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The declaration was made within the prescribed one-year period; its publication in the official gazette after that period did not make the acquisition proceedings invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the one-year limit applies to making the declaration that the land is needed for a public purpose. Section 6(2) requires publication of the declaration but prescribes no time limit for that publication. The Court relied on S.H. Rangappa v. State of Karnataka, Khadim Hussain v. State of U.P., and Sriniwas Ramnath Khatod v. State of Maharashtra.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and official_notification_published and declaration_made_within_one_year and declaration_published_after_one_year

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.official_notification_published: The government published the acquisition notification in the official gazette.
predicates.declaration_made_within_one_year: The government made the declaration that the land was needed within one year of the legally relevant publication of the acquisition notification.
predicates.declaration_published_after_one_year: The declaration was published after one year had passed, although it had been made within that period.

issues.definition: When an acquisition notification has been officially published and the government makes the required declaration within one year, later publication of that declaration does not prevent it from being timely.

issues.legal_issue: Newspaper publication of an acquisition notice before its publication in the official gazette does not start the period for making the subsequent declaration.
material_facts: Notices relating to the proposed acquisition appeared in local newspapers on 31 March and 1 April 1990, before publication of the acquisition notification in the official gazette on 4 June 1992.
The landowners argued that the earlier newspaper notices should determine the start of the one-year period.
The Court held that the official-gazette publication was mandatory and that the earlier newspaper notices were rightly disregarded for calculating the period.
issues.conclusion: The earlier newspaper notices did not start the one-year period; the official-gazette publication was the necessary starting point for the acquisition process.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires publication of the acquisition notification in the official gazette, as well as publication in newspapers and public notice of its substance. Gazette publication is a condition precedent to the acquisition process. The Court relied on Collector (District Magistrate), Allahabad v. Raja Ram Jaiswal and State of Haryana v. Raghubir Dayal.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.newspaper_notice_precedes_official_publi: A notice about the proposed acquisition appeared in newspapers before the acquisition notification was published in the official gazette.

issues.definition: In a land acquisition proceeding, a newspaper notice that precedes official publication does not start the period for making the subsequent declaration.

issues.legal_issue: Some delay in publishing the substance of an acquisition notification after its official-gazette publication does not by itself invalidate the acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette in June 1992, its substance was posted at conspicuous places in November 1992, and it was later published in local newspapers in May 1993.
The landowners argued that the interval between these publications required the acquisition proceedings to be quashed.
The Court held that, even if there was some delay, the sequence did not require the proceedings to be set aside.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings were not invalid merely because there was some delay in the subsequent publication of the notification’s substance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of Haryana v. Raghubir Dayal, which supports the conclusion that some delay in the sequence of publication does not, by itself, require the acquisition proceedings to be quashed.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.required_publications_occurred: The acquisition notification and its substance were published or notified in the required ways.
predicates.publication_sequence_involved_delay: There was some delay between the required steps for publishing or notifying the substance of the acquisition notification.

issues.definition: When the required publication steps in a land acquisition proceeding occurred, some delay in their sequence does not by itself invalidate the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A substantially delayed challenge to a public-purpose land acquisition may be refused where entertaining it risks prejudice to the beneficiaries of the scheme and planned development.
material_facts: The declaration was published in the official gazette on 24 May 1994, while the landowners filed their writ petitions virtually two years later.
The acquisition was for a residential scheme intended to further planned development and benefit the scheme’s intended beneficiaries.
The Court considered that entertaining the delayed challenges could cause serious prejudice to those beneficiaries and to planned development.
issues.conclusion: The delayed writ challenges ought not to have been entertained, and the High Court should have dismissed them on the ground of delay and laches.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the law of delay and laches in challenges to land acquisition and relied on Reliance Petroleum Ltd. v. Zaver Chand Popatlal Sumaria and Hari Singh v. State of U.P.

rule.if: land_acquisition_writ_challenge and challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay and acquisition_serves_public_scheme and entertaining_challenge_may_cause_prejudice

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: A person has brought a writ challenge to a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The challenge was brought substantially after the acquisition step being challenged.
predicates.acquisition_serves_public_scheme: The land acquisition is for a public scheme, such as a scheme for planned development.
predicates.entertaining_challenge_may_cause_prejudi: Entertaining the challenge may seriously prejudice the scheme’s intended beneficiaries or planned development.

issues.definition: A substantially delayed writ challenge to an acquisition for a public scheme should not be entertained when entertaining it may cause serious prejudice to the scheme’s beneficiaries or planned development.
